label: rem:calculus-up-to-epsilon
title: Calculus survives up to $\varepsilon$: derivatives, integrals, limits
html:
While surreal numbers lack a Hilbert-space completion and canonical Lebesgue measure, a substantial fragment of differential and formal integral calculus lifts to \mathbf{No} up to an infinitesimal correction. We record what works and how classical analysis is recovered via the standard-part map.

1. Differential calculus: Jackson derivative as the native d/dx Fix an infinitesimal \varepsilon \in \mathbf{No} with \varepsilon > 0 and set q = 1 + \varepsilon. The Jackson q-derivative

  d_q f(x) = \frac{f(q x) - f(x)}{(q - 1)\, x} = \frac{f((1+\varepsilon) x) - f(x)}{\varepsilon\, x}

is a native difference quotient on \mathbf{No}. Both numerator and denominator are surreals, and their ratio is well-defined wherever \varepsilon \, x \neq 0. For a standard function f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} lifted polynomially to \mathbf{No}, the classical derivative is recovered as

  \frac{df}{dx}(x_0) = \mathrm{st}\!\left(d_q f(x_0)\right) \qquad (x_0 \in \mathbb{R},\; q = 1 + \varepsilon).

The classical-limit functor, which breaks as an honest limit under surreal replacement, is replaced by the standard-part map composed with evaluation at a specific surreal q. More generally, Berarducci--Mantova (2018) construct a genuine derivation D : \mathbf{No} \to \mathbf{No} extending d/dx on \mathbb{R}, making \mathbf{No} a differential field. Many transcendental identities extend accordingly.

2. Formal integration: antiderivative exists, measure does not Berarducci--Mantova show that \mathbf{No} admits a right inverse to D. For every f \in \mathbf{No} there exists an antiderivative F with D(F) = f. This gives an honest indefinite integral \int f \, dx \in \mathbf{No} for every surreal function, up to a constant of integration.

A definite integral \int_a^b f \, dx agreeing with Lebesgue on \mathbb{R}-valued inputs does not exist. We use d_q as the native derivative and reserve \int for either the categorical Frobenius integral or the standard-part of Riemann sums computed on \mathbf{No}-valued partitions.

3. Limits become evaluations Every classical sequential limit L = \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n translates to L = \mathrm{st}(a_\omega), where \omega \in \mathbf{No} is the first infinite ordinal and a_\omega is the surreal obtained by transfer of the formula defining a_n. Limits become named values rather than formal processes. \lim_{q \to 1} becomes evaluation at q = 1 + \varepsilon, and the classical result is the standard-part. Double limits and iterated sup/inf over uncountable index sets require care.

4. Formal power series: the safe regime All formal-power-series identities used in the main paper (\exp_q, \log_q, \mathrm{Li}_2^q, quantum dilogarithm, character generating functions) lift directly because they are manipulations in K[[x]] for K = \mathbf{No}. Convergence is replaced by formal convergence. The information-theory chapter computations survive: entropies, Lyapunov exponents, and bandwidth formulas are rational or formal-power-series expressions in q.

5. Measure up to \varepsilon: Loeb construction Given a hyperfinite partition of [0, 1] \subset \mathbf{No} into N = \omega equal subintervals, the counting measure divided by N gives a hyperfinite measure on [0,1]_{\mathbf{No}}. Its standard-part is Lebesgue measure on [0, 1] \subset \mathbb{R}. This Loeb measure is not canonical but behaves well for standard integrands. For the Möbius energy integral, one can define a Loeb measure on S^1 \times S^1 \subset \mathbf{No}^2, evaluate the integrand 1/|x - y|^2 against it, and take the standard-part after subtracting the regulariser. To infinitesimal precision, this yields the classical Möbius energy.

See Table.

For the substrate-parameter q \to 1 limit, the surreal framework sharpens the theory by naming the infinitesimal regime explicitly. The absence of a canonical Lebesgue measure and a Hilbert completion is manageable because QOU uses neither in a load-bearing way: integration is categorical (Frobenius counit), decomposition is algebraic (Hoefsmit), and analytic-looking quantities (d_H(q), c_q, \hbar_q) are rational in q.
